sections.h2: How should a Carteret owner start planning a sale?
sections.html:
Begin with the borough's occupancy inspection and a current tax bill, because a Carteret sale can go through an agent, a for-sale-by-owner listing or an investor and all three paths pass the same two checkpoints. After those, the deed gets filed in New Brunswick at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry.

About 55 percent of Carteret homes are lived in by their owners, which leaves a large share of the housing stock as rentals. Sellers therefore include landlords, heirs and people with older houses and repairs put off. For those owners the paperwork below weighs as much as the listing photos, and it is worth reading before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: Where is Carteret and what is the housing like?
sections.html:
Carteret sits in northeastern Middlesex County, on the Arthur Kill across from Staten Island, with the Rahway River forming its northern edge against Linden. Woodbridge Township touches it on every land side. The borough began in 1906 as Roosevelt, carved out of Woodbridge after a referendum, and took the Carteret name in 1922 after an early proprietor of the province. Local place names still in use include Chrome, Lamar, Canda, Silvan Beach and West Carteret, the part west of the Turnpike.

Census Bureau estimates show who owns and who rents. Figures come from the latest five-year survey unless the row says otherwise.

  • Residents, mid-2025 estimate: 25,781
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 54.7%
  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $405,800
  • Typical gross rent: $2,032
  • Households: 8,224
  • People per household: 3.10
  • Household income, midpoint: $96,862

Households average more than three people, against 2.53 nationally, and roughly nine in ten residents stayed in the same home over the previous year. The borough's occupancy form has separate lines for one-family and two-family houses, and a house with a clean certificate and working mechanicals gives a buyer fewer reasons to renegotiate.

sections.h2: How do roads, the waterfront and the local economy affect a Carteret sale?
sections.html:
Access is the strength here, though some buyers will want to talk about truck traffic. The New Jersey Turnpike is the only major highway through the borough, with Interchange 12 inside its limits. NJ Transit local buses run the 116 route toward Midtown Manhattan and Perth Amboy and the 48 route toward Elizabeth. The Census Bureau's average commute is 31.4 minutes.

The economy leans toward moving goods. Census data show about $592 million in 2022 transportation and warehousing receipts for Carteret, against roughly $901 million in retail sales. With an economy built around freight and warehousing, buyers may ask about noise, truck routes and flood exposure along the Arthur Kill and Rahway River edges. Walk the block at rush hour before you price the house so you can answer honestly.

  • Know how far the house sits from the Turnpike ramps and from CR 602.
  • Pull together any flood or sump-pump history, since tidal water borders the east side.
  • Keep the block and lot number handy, because every borough form asks for it.

sections.h2: What does the borough require before a Carteret house can close?
sections.html:
Carteret requires a residential certificate of continued occupancy, issued by the Department of Code Enforcement at 61 Cooke Avenue, before a house changes hands. The application asks for the owner, the purchaser, the realtor if there is one, the block and lot, one family or two, the listed price and the names and ages of everyone living there. Code enforcement answers at (732) 541-3925, and inspections are booked through (732) 541-3810.

An addendum to the application works as a plain checklist, and the inspector holds you to it. The seller certifies each item, and the form warns that false statements can be prosecuted with a fine of $2,000 per occurrence.

  • Smoke detectors on each level, plus a smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area, within ten feet.
  • Battery-powered units that carry sealed 10-year batteries.
  • A 2A:10BC fire extinguisher mounted near the kitchen, also within ten feet.
  • Working heat, hot water, electric, water and sewer.
  • No unpermitted work and no open permits.
  • Exterior, grounds, concrete, asphalt and masonry free of disrepair and trip hazards.

The fees are printed on the application itself.

Charges and limits printed on the Carteret occupancy application
ItemAmount or rule on the form
Inspection, one-family house$100
Inspection, two-family house$150
Temporary certificate$75
Name change on an existing certificate$50
Added inspection after a failure or no-show$50 each
Life of the applicationVoid 90 days after issuance

The base fee pays for the first visit and one follow-up. Since the application lapses after 90 days, file it close to your expected closing rather than months ahead. The form lists cash, certified check, or an attorney or broker check as payment, and the borough reserves the right to inspect again later.

sections.h2: What happens with Carteret's tax bills at closing?
sections.html:
The borough mails one tax bill a year, in July, with stubs for the installments due on the first day of February, May, August and November. Finance allows ten days of grace after each date. After that, late installments accrue 8 percent a year on up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any larger amount, counted from the original due date. A delinquency above $10,000 also draws a 6 percent year-end penalty, and balances left open for a year or more are swept into the annual tax sale.

The borough's own advice is to have the latest bill at the closing table, because the buyer's side needs the next installment amount. The tax collector works from the finance department at 100 Cooke Avenue on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Call (732) 541-3820 extension 3818 for a payoff figure.

If you believe the assessment is off, take it up with the borough assessor first, at extension 3110. Next comes an appeal package from the Middlesex County Tax Board in New Brunswick. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 in a revalued town, and the owner must show the assessed value is unreasonable next to market value. People who hold a senior or veteran deduction also send in an annual statement by March 1 to keep it.

sections.h2: How does Middlesex County record the deed, and which tax forms apply?
sections.html:
Carteret deeds are filed at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick. The office serves the public on weekdays and asks visitors to arrive by 4 p.m. Your attorney or title company usually handles the filing. The county's online search reaches back to 1929 for deeds and 1950 for mortgages, so you can pull your own chain of title before listing, although staff do not run title searches.

Per the county's schedule, a deed costs $45 for page one and $10 for each added page, with a $6 name fee after the fifth name. State charges sit on top of those: the seller owes the realty transfer fee, and every seller hands over a gross income tax form. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification and settles income tax on the regular return. An out-of-state seller, including a former Carteret resident who has relocated, prepays either two percent of the price or the 8.97 percent rate applied to net gain, unless an exemption listed on the form fits.

Federal rules let an owner keep $250,000 of profit free of tax, or $500,000 for a married couple, after living in the home two of the previous five years, and the state follows that approach.

sections.h2: Which routes get a Carteret house sold fastest?
sections.html:
The quickest routes are a cash purchase from an investor or a short listing of a well-prepared house, and the borough certificate gates both. A cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting, yet the inspection, the tax payoff and the deed filing still apply.

  • Choose an agent if the house is in good shape and you can sit through showings and a lender's calendar.
  • Choose an as-is investor sale if the house needs work, has tenants, carries back taxes or belongs to an estate.
  • Choose a sale by owner only with an attorney lined up for the contract, the certificate and the closing forms.

Whichever way you go, order the inspection early, replace alarms and the extinguisher yourself, and ask the buyer's attorney who will book the final walk-through. If a repair cannot be finished before the closing date, ask the borough code office whether a temporary certificate is available.

faqs.q: Is an occupancy inspection mandatory for Carteret sellers?
faqs.a: Yes. The Department of Code Enforcement issues a residential certificate of continued occupancy after an inspection, and the application lapses 90 days after issuance, so time it close to closing.

faqs.q: How much does the Carteret inspection run?
faqs.a: The borough form lists $100 for a one-family house and $150 for a two-family house. A temporary certificate is $75, and every extra inspection after a failure or no-show is $50.

faqs.q: What are Carteret's quarterly tax dates?
faqs.a: Installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, with ten days of grace. Late balances accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 and 18 percent on anything above that.

faqs.q: Which Middlesex County office files a Carteret deed?
faqs.a: The County Clerk's Registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick. A closing attorney or title agent usually delivers it with the state transfer and income tax forms.

faqs.q: Can a Carteret house with tenants or open repairs still sell?
faqs.a: Yes, but the occupancy inspection still applies and the application lists everyone living in the home. Ask the code office about open permits first, since the form requires that none be open.
